exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with calf claudication after walking 50 m. What is the next investigative step and why? — ABI; values < 0.9 confirm PAD and guide further imaging.

During knee replacement, the surgeon notes a pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Popliteal artery aneurysm; obtain vascular surgery consult and arrange duplex ultrasound.

A patient with a distal femur fracture has a weak popliteal pulse but normal femoral pulse. What does this suggest and what should you do? — Possible arterial injury; immobilise limb, call vascular team, arrange urgent imaging.
Explain why the genicular arteries are important when the knee is flexed. — They provide collateral flow, preventing ischemia when the main popliteal lumen is compressed.

A diabetic patient presents with a cold foot and absent dorsalis pedis pulse but a palpable popliteal pulse. What is the likely level of obstruction? — Occlusion distal to the popliteal bifurcation, likely tibial artery disease.

Why is a CT angiogram preferred over plain X‑ray in evaluating a suspected popliteal artery injury? — CT angiogram visualises vessel lumen, detects intimal flaps and pseudo‑aneurysms, which X‑ray cannot.

In a low‑resource clinic, how would you monitor a patient with a known popliteal aneurysm? — Serial clinical measurement of mass size, pulse assessment, and ABI; refer for surgery if rapid growth or symptoms develop.

What drug class should be avoided in a patient with a popliteal artery aneurysm undergoing elective repair and why? — Non‑selective NSAIDs; they impair platelet function and increase bleeding risk during surgery.
ai.title: Popliteal Artery Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee, supplying the lower leg and foot. Its course, branches and relationships are crucial for diagnosing trauma, aneurysm and peripheral arterial disease, especially where imaging is limited.

b: Key landmark: adductor hiatus of the femur
Divides at the level of the tibial tuberosity
sections.p: The popliteal artery runs in the popliteal fossa from the adductor hiatus to the lower border of the popliteus muscle where it divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

b: Surrounded by the popliteal fascia and fat
sections.p: It lies deep in the fossa, initially superficial to the popliteal vein, then deep to it as it descends. The artery is a muscular vessel about 15 cm long.

b: Popliteal vein lies superficial early, then deep
Tibial nerve runs medial to the artery
sections.p: Anteriorly the artery is bordered by the popliteus muscle; posteriorly by the popliteal vein and tibial nerve. The small saphenous vein pierces the fascia near the medial head of gastrocnemius.

b: Genicular arteries maintain knee perfusion during flexion
Anterior tibial artery supplies the dorsum of the foot
sections.p: Branches include the genicular arteries (superior, middle, inferior) that form an anastomotic network around the knee, the sural arteries, and the anterior/posterior tibial arteries.
The arterial wall receives sympathetic fibers from the lumbar sympathetic chain via the hypogastric plexus; no direct somatic innervation.

b: Palpable popliteal pulse predicts intact tibial pulses
sections.p: Delivers oxygenated blood to the knee joint, posterior compartment of the leg, and foot; its pulsation is a bedside indicator of distal perfusion.

b: Aneurysm: pulsatile mass, absent distal pulses, risk of thrombosis
Trauma: popliteal fracture or dislocation can transect the artery
PAD: calf claudication, cold foot, delayed capillary refill
sections.p: Trauma, popliteal artery aneurysm, and peripheral arterial disease (PAD) are the main threats. In low‑resource settings, delayed presentation and limited imaging increase limb‑loss risk.

t.b: Is there hemodynamic obstruction? ABI < 0.9 indicates PAD; if Doppler unavailable, use handheld Doppler or clinical pulse‑pressure assessment
Is there aneurysm or stenosis? Shows flow velocity; if ultrasound unavailable, rely on palpable pulse asymmetry and bedside Doppler
What is the exact anatomy before surgery? Shows branch involvement; if CT unavailable, consider plain X‑ray for fracture and clinical assessment

b: Check femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses
Compare limb temperatures and capillary refill
Look for a pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa
sections.p: When assessing a patient with suspected popliteal pathology, start with a systematic vascular exam and then consider the most likely local causes.

whenToSeekHelp: Absent distal pulses with a painful, swollen knee after trauma
Severe calf pain with pallor and paresthesia (suspected acute limb ischemia)
